library(here)

# 1. What is in `Data/otters_USGS`?
Exploring data packages from USGS (various citations) and listing data files used: 

Hatfield, B.B., Yee, J.L., Kenner, M.C., and Tomoleoni, J.A., 2019, Annual California sea otter census - 2019 spring census summary: U.S. Geological Survey data release, https://doi.org/10.5066/P9B2KNB3.

Tinker, M.T., and Hatfield, B.B., 2018, Annual California sea otter census—1985-2014 spring census summary: U.S. Geological Survey data release, https://doi.org/10.5066/F7445JQ5.

Hatfield, B.B., Yee, J.L., Kenner, M.C., Tomoleoni, J.A., and Tinker, M.T., 2018, Annual California sea otter census—2018 spring census summary: U.S. Geological Survey data release, https://doi.org/10.5066/P98012HE.

Tinker, M.T., and Hatfield, B.B., 2017, Annual California sea otter census—2017 spring census summary: U.S. Geological Survey data release, https://doi.org/10.5066/F7R2109J.

Tinker, M.T., and Hatfield, B.B., 2016, Annual California Sea Otter Census - 2016 Spring Census Summary: U.S. Geological Survey data release, http://dx.doi.org/10.5066/F7FJ2DWJ.

Tinker, M.T., and Hatfield, B.B., 2015, Southwest U.S. Southern sea otter annual range-wide census results: U.S. Geological Survey data release, http://dx.doi.org/10.5066/F7F47M5C.


| File | What it is | Years | Geometry? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `5a32d390e4b08e6a89d88583.csv` | Census-summary **time series**: one row per habitat polygon x year (ScienceBase item `5a32d390e4b08e6a89d88583`) | 1985-2014 (no 2011) | **No.** Attributes only, keyed by `POLY_ID` |
| `Spring2014_SeaOtterCensus/Census_sum_14.shp` | 2014 census-summary polygons | 2014 | Polygons, CA Teale Albers (EPSG:3310) |
| `Spring2014_SeaOtterCensus/Census_sum.xls` | Same attributes as the 2014 shapefile, as a table | 2014 | No |
| `Spring2014_SeaOtterCensus/Range_counts.xls` | **Raw** 2014 spring count per ATOS point (single year, not averaged) | 2014 | No (ATOS id only) |
| `Spring2014_SeaOtterCensus/Extra_limit_obs_14.shp` / `Extra_lim_counts.xls` | 3 otters seen outside the official range limits | 2014 | Points (has lat/long) |
| `Spring2014_SeaOtterCensus/Range_extent_14.shp` | Line showing the 2014 mainland range | 2014 | Line |
| `Census_sum_2019/Census_sum_2019.shp` | 2019 census-summary polygons | 2019 | Polygons, EPSG:3310 |


## from the FGDC metadata (`*_FGDC.xml`)

* **ATOS** ("As The Otter Swims") points are spaced about every 500 m along the coast. ATOS 0 is at the Golden Gate and ATOS 2024 at the Mexico border, and the numbers increase from north to south.
* Each ATOS point has up to two habitat **polygons**. `ZONE_CODE` **n** is nearshore (0 to 30 m depth). **o** is offshore (30 to 60 m, or within 10 km of shore). There are also a few **b** (bay/slough) and **w** (way offshore) polygons. `POLY_ID` / `HAB_ID` = ATOS id + zone letter, e.g. `321n`.
* **`dens_sm`**: the *3-year average* number of otters per km^2 in the polygon, smoothed over 10 km of coastline.
* **`lin_dens`**: the *3-year average* otters per ATOS segment, also 10 km-smoothed. It is shared by the n and o polygons of one ATOS.
* **`pupratio`**: pups / independents, 3-yr average, smoothed.
* **`trend5yr`**: the local exponential growth rate over the previous 5 years, smoothed.
* `AREA` is in km^2, `PERIMETER` in km.

> **caveat:** these files do **not** contain raw counts (except
> `Range_counts.xls`). Every polygon value is *already* a 3-year running
> average. So the **2019 file is the 2017-2019 average**, (the
> index USGS and USFWS recommend).

# 2. read csvs

```{r read}
otter_dir <- here::here("Data", "otters_USGS")

census_ts <- read_csv(file.path(otter_dir, "5a32d390e4b08e6a89d88583.csv"))

shp14 <- st_read(file.path(otter_dir, "Spring2014_SeaOtterCensus", "Census_sum_14.shp"), quiet = TRUE)
shp19 <- st_read(file.path(otter_dir, "Census_sum_2019", "Census_sum_2019.shp"), quiet = TRUE)

```

## Read every yearly census-summary shapefile

USGS releases one summary shapefile per year, and the folder/file names and column names vary a little between releases. Rather than reading each year by hand, the function below:

* finds **every** `.shp` under `Data/otters_USGS/` and keeps only the census summaries (files with a density column). The range-extent and extra-limit files are skipped.
* matches column names case-insensitively (`dens_sm` = `DENS_SM`) and uses `HAB_ID` when `POLY_ID` is missing.
* takes the year from the `Year` column. If that is missing, it reads it from the file name (`2018` or `_15` -> 2015).
* returns a table with the same columns as the CSV time series, so the two can be stacked.

Adding a new year later = drop its folder into `Data/otters_USGS/` and re-knit. No code changes.

```{r read-all-summaries}
std_cols <- c("Year", "POLY_ID", "HAB_ID", "ATOS_ID", "ZONE_CODE", "AREA",
              "dens_sm", "lin_dens", "pupratio", "trend5yr")

read_census_summary <- function(f) {
  d <- st_drop_geometry(st_read(f, quiet = TRUE))

  # case-insensitive rename to the standard column names
  for (nm in std_cols) {
    hit <- names(d)[tolower(names(d)) == tolower(nm)]
    if (length(hit) == 1 && hit != nm) names(d)[names(d) == hit] <- nm
  }
  if (!"dens_sm" %in% names(d)) return(NULL)        # not a census summary (range line, extra-limit points)

  if (!"POLY_ID" %in% names(d)) d$POLY_ID <- d$HAB_ID
  if (!"AREA" %in% names(d) && "HECTARES" %in% names(d)) d$AREA <- d$HECTARES / 100   # km^2

  # year: from the data if present, otherwise from the file name
  if (!"Year" %in% names(d) || all(is.na(d$Year))) {
    yr4 <- str_extract(basename(f), "(19|20)\\d{2}")
    yr2 <- str_match(basename(f), "_(\\d{2})\\.shp$")[, 2]
    d$Year <- if (!is.na(yr4)) as.numeric(yr4) else 2000 + as.numeric(yr2)
  }

  for (nm in setdiff(std_cols, names(d))) d[[nm]] <- NA   # e.g. a release without trend5yr

  d %>%
    transmute(Year = as.numeric(Year), POLY_ID = as.character(POLY_ID),
              ATOS_ID = as.numeric(ATOS_ID), ZONE_CODE, AREA = as.numeric(AREA),
              dens_sm, lin_dens, pupratio, trend5yr,
              source = file.path(basename(dirname(f)), basename(f)))
}

shp_files  <- list.files(otter_dir, pattern = "\\.shp$", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)
census_shp <- map_dfr(shp_files, read_census_summary)

# What was found (one row per file)
census_shp %>%
  group_by(Year, source) %>%
  summarise(n_polygons = n(), index_3yr = round(sum(dens_sm * AREA)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(Year)

# If two files claim the same year, keep the first and say so
dup_years <- census_shp %>% distinct(Year, source) %>% count(Year) %>% filter(n > 1)
if (nrow(dup_years) > 0) warning("More than one shapefile for year(s): ",
                                 paste(dup_years$Year, collapse = ", "), ". Keeping the first.")
census_shp <- census_shp %>%
  group_by(Year) %>% filter(source == first(source)) %>% ungroup()

# One long table, all years: CSV for 1985-2014, shapefiles for every year the CSV doesn't have
census_all <- census_ts %>%
  transmute(Year, POLY_ID, ATOS_ID, ZONE_CODE, AREA, dens_sm, lin_dens, pupratio, trend5yr,
            source = "CSV time series") %>%
  bind_rows(filter(census_shp, !Year %in% census_ts$Year)) %>%
  mutate(otters_3yr = dens_sm * AREA,
         avg_window = paste0(Year - 2, "-", Year)) %>%
  arrange(Year)

census_all %>% count(Year, source) %>% print(n = Inf)
```

**Check that AREA means the same thing in every release.** AREA should be km^2 everywhere. If a release used different units, the ratio to the 2019 polygon areas would be far from 1 and its index would be off by that factor.

```{r area-check}
census_all %>%
  inner_join(st_drop_geometry(shp19) %>% select(POLY_ID = HAB_ID, AREA_2019 = AREA), by = "POLY_ID") %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  summarise(median_area_ratio = round(median(AREA / AREA_2019), 3)) %>%
  filter(Year >= 2010)
```
## structure checks

```{r structure}
# rows (polygons) per year in the time series
census_ts %>% count(Year) %>% print(n = Inf)

# 2019 columns differ slightly: it has 'id' and no 'POLY_ID' / 'Sect_ID'
setdiff(names(shp14), names(shp19))
setdiff(names(shp19), names(shp14))

# Same polygon IDs?  Is every 2014 polygon also in 2019?
all(shp14$HAB_ID %in% shp19$HAB_ID)
setdiff(shp19$HAB_ID, shp14$HAB_ID)   # extra 2019 polys = range expansion (south end)

# Does the CSV's 2014 slice equal the 2014 shapefile?
census_ts %>% filter(Year == 2014) %>%
  inner_join(st_drop_geometry(shp14) %>% select(POLY_ID, dens_sm_shp = dens_sm), by = "POLY_ID") %>%
  summarise(n = n(), max_abs_diff = max(abs(dens_sm - dens_sm_shp)))
```
So the CSV and the shapefiles share **one polygon framework**: the same `POLY_ID`/`HAB_ID` and the same shapes. You can attach geometry to any CSV year by joining on `POLY_ID`.

## sanity check: density x area ~ the 3-year population index
since density is a per km sq index, I wnat the overall pop back per polygon (unit area)

```{r index-check}
index_ts <- census_all %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  summarise(index_3yr = sum(otters_3yr))

index_ts %>% tail(8)

# years with no point, for the subtitle
missing_years <- setdiff(min(index_ts$Year):max(index_ts$Year), index_ts$Year)

ggplot(index_ts, aes(Year, index_3yr)) +
  # marine heatwave band, drawn first so it sits behind the line and points
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2014, xmax = 2015, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "red", alpha = 0.15) +

  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  
  # a tick for every year, but a label only every 5 years
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1985, 2020, 5),
                     minor_breaks = 1985:2020,
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0.01)) +
  guides(x = guide_axis(minor.ticks = TRUE)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  
  labs(y = "Sum of dens_sm x AREA (otters)",
       title = "Mainland 3-yr average index rebuilt from polygon densities",
       subtitle = if (length(missing_years) > 0)
         paste0("No data for: ", paste(missing_years, collapse = ", "), " (red band = MHW)") else NULL) +

  theme(axis.ticks.x = element_line(colour = "grey30"),
        axis.ticks.length.x = unit(4, "pt"),
        axis.minor.ticks.length.x = rel(0.8),   # yearly ticks a bit shorter than the 5-yr ones
        panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank())   # no yearly gridlines

#ggsave(here::here("Outputs", "otters", "Total_popluation_avgs.png"), width = 9, height = 7)
```

The sums come out at about 2,881 for 2014 and 2,863 for 2019. These are the published *mainland* 3-year averages (the headline USGS numbers also add San Nicolas Island). This confirms that **`dens_sm x AREA` = the 3-yr average otters in each polygon**.


# 3. otters at lat/long positions

There are two sensible spatial units:
1. **Polygon centroid** (n and o separately). This keeps the inshore/offshore split.
2. **ATOS point** (n + o summed). One point every 500 m along the coast, which is usually the most useful for joining to survey sites.

I use `st_point_on_surface()` instead of `st_centroid()` so that every point falls inside its (often curved) polygon.

```{r latlong-2019}
otters_2019_poly <- shp19 %>%
  rename(POLY_ID = HAB_ID) %>%
  mutate(otters_3yr = dens_sm * AREA,     # 3-yr avg otters in polygon (2017-2019)
         avg_window = "2017-2019") %>%
  st_point_on_surface() %>%
  st_transform(4326) %>%
  mutate(lon = st_coordinates(.)[, 1],
         lat = st_coordinates(.)[, 2])

# Collapse to ATOS points (sum n + o). The geometry is the mean of the polygon points.
otters_2019_atos <- otters_2019_poly %>%
  group_by(ATOS_ID) %>%
  summarise(otters_3yr = sum(otters_3yr),
            lin_dens   = first(lin_dens),   # alt. per-ATOS index (excludes bay polys)
            pupratio   = first(pupratio),
            trend5yr   = first(trend5yr),
            do_union = TRUE) %>%
  st_centroid() %>%
  mutate(lon = st_coordinates(.)[, 1],
         lat = st_coordinates(.)[, 2],
         Year = 2019, avg_window = "2017-2019")

head(st_drop_geometry(otters_2019_atos))

# compare the two per-ATOS measures
otters_2019_atos %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(diff = otters_3yr - lin_dens) %>%
  summarise(total_area_based = sum(otters_3yr), total_lin_dens = sum(lin_dens),
            median_abs_diff = median(abs(diff)), max_abs_diff = max(abs(diff)))
otters_2019_atos %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(diff = otters_3yr - lin_dens) %>% arrange(desc(abs(diff))) %>% head(4)
```
**Area-based (`dens_sm x AREA`) vs `lin_dens`.** Range-wide the two totals are the same, but at single ATOS points they differ (median ~ 0.3 otters).

* The large differences are the **bay polygons**: ATOS 321 (Elkhorn Slough, about 100 otters) and ATOS 826 (Morro Bay). `lin_dens` leaves those otters out of the coastline value.
* Elsewhere, the 10 km smoothing spreads otters a little differently between neighbouring points. This doesn't matter once you sum over a few km.

Use `otters_3yr` (area-based) if you want bay otters included.

**Basemaps.** Free state outlines (e.g. the `maps` package) are too coarse for this coastline: they put the shore 1-3 km from where it really is, so points look like they sit on land. The zoomed maps use **USGS habitat polygons themselves** as the background so they line up exactly with the points. The landward edge of the nearshore polygons is the shoreline, and the bay polygons trace Elkhorn Slough and Morro Bay.

The full-state map still uses the `maps` California outline (`install.packages("maps")`) for context. At that scale the offset is smaller than a point. For a true land layer at any zoom, `tigris::states(cb = TRUE)` (US Census 1:500k) is accurate enough.

```{r ca-basemap}
ca <- st_as_sf(maps::map("state", regions = "california", plot = FALSE, fill = TRUE)) %>%
  st_transform(4326)

zone_labels <- c(n = "Nearshore (0-30 m)", o = "Offshore (30-60 m)",
                 b = "Bay / slough", w = "Way offshore (>10 km)")

# USGS habitat polygons as the coastline background (exactly registered with the points)
habitat_bg <- shp19 %>%
  filter(ZONE_CODE != "w") %>%          # single 'way offshore' polygon; not needed for the outline
  st_transform(4326) %>%
  # named 'hab_zone' (not 'zone') so the background is drawn in every facet of faceted maps
  mutate(hab_zone = factor(zone_labels[ZONE_CODE], levels = zone_labels))

habitat_fill <- scale_fill_manual(values = c("Nearshore (0-30 m)" = "#b9d7ee",
                                             "Offshore (30-60 m)" = "#e1edf7",
                                             "Bay / slough"       = "#b9dfc6"),
                                  name = "Habitat zone", drop = TRUE)

# Range-scale maps: dissolve the ~2,000 polygons into one band per zone so there are
# no internal edges. The band's landward edge is the coastline.
habitat_band <- habitat_bg %>%
  group_by(hab_zone) %>%
  summarise(do_union = TRUE) %>%
  st_make_valid()

habitat_layer <- list(
  geom_sf(data = habitat_band, aes(fill = hab_zone), colour = "grey45", linewidth = 0.25),
  habitat_fill
)

# Close-up maps: keep the individual polygon outlines
habitat_layer_detail <- list(
  geom_sf(data = habitat_bg, aes(fill = hab_zone), colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.15, alpha = 0.7),
  habitat_fill
)

# ---- What counts as "zero"? -------------------------------------------------
# The 10 km smoothing spreads fractional otters along the coast, so very few points
# are exactly 0 (2019: 8 of 993 ATOS points, 15 nearshore and 346 offshore polygons).
# zero_cutoff = 0   -> only exact zeros are white
# zero_cutoff = 0.5 -> anything under half an otter is white as well (~230 more ATOS points)
zero_cutoff <- 0
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Split ATOS points into zero and non-zero. Zeros are drawn in white, off the viridis
# scale, so the colour range only covers points that actually have otters.
# Sort so the highest values are drawn on top.
otters_2019_map <- otters_2019_atos %>%
  filter(otters_3yr > zero_cutoff) %>%
  arrange(otters_3yr)

otters_2019_map0 <- otters_2019_atos %>%
  filter(otters_3yr <= zero_cutoff)

# White points with a thin grey outline (a grey point drawn slightly larger underneath),
# so zeros stay visible on the white background and the light-blue habitat band.
# Add this layer BEFORE the coloured points so zeros sit underneath.
zero_points <- function(data, size, mapping = NULL) {
  list(
    geom_sf(data = data, mapping = mapping, colour = "grey40", size = size + 0.6),
    geom_sf(data = data, mapping = mapping, colour = "white",  size = size)
  )
}

otter_scale <- scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "otters / ATOS\n(3-yr avg)",
                                      direction = -1)   # low = light yellow, high = dark
```

```{r map-2019-state, fig.height=7, fig.width=6}
# Whole state, for context
bb <- st_bbox(otters_2019_atos)   # all points, including zeros at the range tips
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = ca, fill = "grey92", colour = "grey50") +
  habitat_layer +
  zero_points(otters_2019_map0, size = 0.8) +
  geom_sf(data = otters_2019_map, aes(colour = otters_3yr), size = 0.8) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = bb["xmin"] - 0.15, xmax = bb["xmax"] + 0.15,
           ymin = bb["ymin"] - 0.15, ymax = bb["ymax"] + 0.15,
           fill = NA, colour = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
  otter_scale +
  labs(title = "Southern sea otter, 2017-2019 3-yr average",
       subtitle = paste0("black box shows area of USGS census summary 2019 (2017-2019)")) +
  theme_minimal()

#ggsave(here::here("Outputs", "otters", "whole_state_2019.png"))
```

```{r map-2019-zoom, fig.height=7, fig.width=7}
# Zoomed to the otter range (the dashed box above)
ggplot() +
  habitat_layer +
  zero_points(otters_2019_map0, size = 1) +
  geom_sf(data = otters_2019_map, aes(colour = otters_3yr), size = 1) +
  otter_scale +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(bb["xmin"] - 0.15, bb["xmax"] + 0.15),
           ylim = c(bb["ymin"] - 0.15, bb["ymax"] + 0.15), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Southern sea otter range, 2017-2019 3-yr average",
       subtitle = paste0("USGS census summary 2019; white points = ", zero_cutoff, " otters or fewer"),
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave(here::here("Outputs", "otters", "zoom_2019.png"))
```

## Nearshore vs offshore vs bay polygons (2017-2019 dataset)

Here every **polygon** is its own point, not summed to ATOS. Each ATOS point usually has two: nearshore (`n`, 0-30 m) and offshore (`o`, 30-60 m). Elkhorn Slough (ATOS 321) and Morro Bay (ATOS 826) also have a third, bay (`b`), polygon. Polygons with 0 otters are shown as white points, off the colour scale.

The colour scale is square-root transformed (Otherwise the ~100 otters in Elkhorn Slough make every other point look the same.)

```{r zone-prep}
otters_2019_zone <- otters_2019_poly %>%
  filter(otters_3yr > zero_cutoff) %>%
  mutate(zone = factor(zone_labels[ZONE_CODE], levels = zone_labels)) %>%
  arrange(otters_3yr)

# Zero polygons (white points). The single 'way offshore' polygon (900w, 0 otters)
# is left out so it doesn't add a fourth facet.
otters_2019_zone0 <- otters_2019_poly %>%
  filter(otters_3yr <= zero_cutoff, ZONE_CODE != "w") %>%
  mutate(zone = factor(zone_labels[ZONE_CODE], levels = zone_labels))

zone_scale <- scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "otters / polygon\n(3-yr avg)",
                                     direction = -1, trans = "sqrt",
                                     breaks = c(1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100))

# How the otters split between zones
otters_2019_poly %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(ZONE_CODE) %>%
  summarise(n_polygons = n(), otters = round(sum(otters_3yr)),
            pct = round(100 * sum(otters_3yr) / sum(otters_2019_poly$otters_3yr), 1))
```

```{r map-2019-zones, fig.height=7, fig.width=11}
facet_order <- c("Offshore (30-60 m)", "Nearshore (0-30 m)", "Bay / slough")

ggplot() +
  habitat_layer +
  zero_points(mutate(otters_2019_zone0, zone = factor(zone, levels = facet_order)), size = 0.9) +
  geom_sf(data = mutate(otters_2019_zone, zone = factor(zone, levels = facet_order)),
          aes(colour = otters_3yr), size = 0.9) +
  zone_scale +
  facet_wrap(~ zone, nrow = 1, drop = TRUE) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(bb["xmin"] - 0.15, bb["xmax"] + 0.15),
           ylim = c(bb["ymin"] - 0.15, bb["ymax"] + 0.15), expand = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-122, -121)) +
  labs(title = "Otters by habitat zone, 2017-2019 3-yr average",
       subtitle = paste0("One point per census polygon; white points = ", zero_cutoff, " otters or fewer"),
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

#ggsave(here::here("Outputs", "otters", "zone_comparison.png"), width = 11)
```
At full-range scale the nearshore and offshore points of one ATOS sit almost on top of each other, so this close-up of Monterey Bay shows them side by side. Elkhorn Slough is the third point inland at Moss Landing.

```{r map-2019-zones-monterey, fig.height=7, fig.width=7}
ggplot() +
  habitat_layer_detail +
  zero_points(otters_2019_zone0, size = 2.2, mapping = aes(shape = zone)) +
  geom_sf(data = otters_2019_zone, aes(colour = otters_3yr, shape = zone), size = 2.2) +
  zone_scale +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Nearshore (0-30 m)" = 16, "Offshore (30-60 m)" = 17,
                                "Bay / slough" = 15, "Way offshore (>10 km)" = 4),
                     name = "Zone") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-122.05, -121.70), ylim = c(36.50, 36.90), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Monterey Bay (incl Elkhorn Slough): polygons by zone, 2017-2019",
       subtitle = paste0("White points = ", zero_cutoff, " otters or fewer"), x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r map-2019-zones-morro, fig.height=7, fig.width=7}
ggplot() +
  habitat_layer_detail +
  zero_points(otters_2019_zone0, size = 2.2, mapping = aes(shape = zone)) +
  geom_sf(data = otters_2019_zone, aes(colour = otters_3yr, shape = zone), size = 2.2) +
  zone_scale +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Nearshore (0-30 m)" = 16, "Offshore (30-60 m)" = 17,
                                "Bay / slough" = 15, "Way offshore (>10 km)" = 4),
                     name = "Zone") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-121.0, -120.75), ylim = c(35.25, 35.50), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Morro Bay: polygons by zone, 2017-2019",
       subtitle = paste0("White points = ", zero_cutoff, " otters or fewer"), x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# 4. Full time series with lat/long (all years)

`census_all` (section 2) already holds every year: the CSV for 1985-2014 and the yearly shapefiles after that.

The 2019 shapefile holds the largest polygon set, so I use it as the geometry lookup. A few older polygons (about 300 IDs, mostly the range tips in 1999-2001 and 2008-2009) are missing from it. They hold very few otters (at most ~44 in any year), and below they are kept with NA coordinates rather than dropped silently.

```{r ts-latlong}
poly_lookup <- otters_2019_poly %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(POLY_ID, ATOS_ID, ZONE_CODE, lon, lat)

otters_ts_poly <- census_all %>%
  left_join(poly_lookup %>% select(POLY_ID, lon, lat), by = "POLY_ID")

# How much is lost without geometry?
otters_ts_poly %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  summarise(otters_no_coords = sum(otters_3yr[is.na(lat)]),
            otters_total     = sum(otters_3yr)) %>%
  filter(otters_no_coords > 0)

# ATOS-level long table: Year x ATOS x lat/lon
atos_lookup <- otters_2019_atos %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(ATOS_ID, lon, lat)

otters_ts_atos <- otters_ts_poly %>%
  group_by(Year, avg_window, ATOS_ID) %>%
  summarise(otters_3yr = sum(otters_3yr),
            pupratio   = first(pupratio),
            trend5yr   = first(trend5yr), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(atos_lookup, by = "ATOS_ID")

glimpse(otters_ts_atos)
```

Pick the panels here. Any year in `census_all` works. For panels with no shared census years, keep them at least 3 years apart, e.g. `c(2010, 2013, 2016, 2019)`.

```{r ts-plot, fig.height=9}
ts_years <- c(1985, 1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2019)

otters_ts_atos %>%
  filter(Year %in% ts_years, !is.na(lat)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(lat, otters_3yr)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ avg_window, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  labs(x = "Latitude (north - south)", y = "otters per ATOS (3-yr avg)") +
  theme_minimal()

#ggsave(here::here("Outputs", "otters", "timeseries_line.png"), width = 10, height = 8)
```
